title: Asynchrony in Python: async/await and when it actually helps

videos.script: People say async makes Python fast. It does not make a single line run faster. {{myth}} What it does is let one process do something useful while it waits. And a web request spends most of its life waiting. For a database. For a partner's API. For a slow phone on a slow network. {{waiting}} Today you build a partner that always takes one second, and you ask it three questions. One after the other, three seconds. All at once, one. {{three}} You watch the event loop at work, switching between coroutines whenever one of them awaits. {{loop}} Then you load a FastAPI route with a hundred requests at once. Written with async def, it holds up. Written with def, it runs out of threads. {{load}} And then the mistake. An async def route with one ordinary blocking call inside. It looks correct. It passes every test you would write. And under load, it stops the whole server. {{blocking}} Last, the case async cannot help at all: work that computes. Four requests take four times as long, whichever way you write them.
